Memory Jogger.new: Rejecting a multi-front attack on the Indian Child Welfare Act, the Court held 7--2 that ICWA falls within Congress's Article~I power over Indian affairs, that its custody rules do not commandeer the States, and that the individual challengers and Texas lacked standing to press equal protection claims against federal officials (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/599/21-376/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court decided the case by a \textbf{7--2} vote. It was argued on November 9, 2022, and decided on June 15, 2023 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/599/21-376/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/21-376}{Cornell LII}). Disposition:

Judicial Votes.src: 994 F.3d 249 affirmed in part (Article I legislative authority), reversed in part (Tenth Amendment anticommandeering), and vacated and remanded in part with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction (equal protection and nondelegation)

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Statute Upheld): A Federal Rule for Tribal Members' Estates.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: Congress enacts a statute requiring ``any party'' petitioning a state probate court over an off-reservation tribal member's intestate estate to show ``active efforts'' to notify the tribe, apply a federal heirloom preference favoring tribal relatives, and have state probate clerks transmit inventories to the Interior Department. Under \textit{Brackeen}, there is no ``probate carveout'' to Article I Indian-affairs power; the ``any party'' rule is evenhanded; the preference validly preempts state law in state courts; clerk reporting is an ancillary judicial duty; and neither a State nor a surviving spouse suing federal officials in federal court has standing to raise an equal protection challenge.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (No Standing): An Adoption Agency Sues the Secretary.} A private adoption agency that places children with non-Indian foster families sues the Secretary of the Interior in federal district court, alleging that ICWA's foster-care preferences in \S~1915(b) disadvantage its families on the basis of race, and seeks a declaratory judgment and an injunction against the Secretary. Under \textit{Brackeen}, the suit must be dismissed for lack of redressability: state courts and state agencies, not the Secretary, apply the placement preferences, so a judgment against the Secretary would not bind the state judges who decide each placement. That a favorable federal opinion might persuade state courts does not count, because it is the judgment, not the opinion, that redresses an injury. The agency's families must raise the claim as parties in a state-court custody proceeding, as Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence noted.
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Statute Invalid): A Nationwide Child-Welfare Mandate Under the Interstate Commerce Clause.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: Now suppose Congress invokes the \emph{Interstate} Commerce Clause to enact a nationwide child-welfare law applying to \emph{all} children that directs ``every State's Department of Child Protective Services'' (and no private actors) to conduct 50-state extended-family searches and orders state legislatures to adopt federal foster-licensing codes. Here, the outcome flips on every axis: (1) under the Interstate Commerce Clause (\textit{Lopez}; \textit{Morrison}), non-economic family custody proceedings lack a commercial nexus, making ``children are not commodities'' dispositive; (2) singling out state agencies and state legislatures directly violates \textit{Printz}, \textit{New York}, and \textit{Murphy}; and (3) the State possesses direct sovereign standing to challenge the federal command.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Provision Likely Invalid): A Search Duty Imposed Only on State Agencies.} Amending ICWA itself, Congress requires each State's child-welfare agency, and no other party, to complete a documented nationwide search for extended-family and tribal placements before any Indian child may enter foster care, and to file monthly search reports with the Secretary of the Interior. Congress's Article~I power over Indian affairs still covers the subject, so the challenge turns on the Tenth Amendment. \textit{Brackeen} upheld \S~1912 because it binds ``any party'' evenhandedly and upheld \S~1915 because, under \textit{Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl}, it imposes no search duty on state agencies. A duty addressed only to state executive agencies, with reporting by agency officials rather than ancillary court recordkeeping, is the kind of direct command to state officers that \textit{Printz} and \textit{Murphy} forbid, so the State would likely prevail.

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Undecided): An Equal Protection Challenge Raised in State Court.} Non-Indian foster parents seek to adopt a child who is eligible for membership in one tribe; a family belonging to a different tribe asks for the placement under \S~1915(a)'s ``other Indian families'' preference. In the state adoption proceeding, where the preference is actually applied, the foster parents argue that it is a racial classification barred by \textit{Palmore v. Sidoti}, 466 U.S. 429 (1984). Their standing is secure, so a court must reach the merits \textit{Brackeen} left open. The tribe answers that, under \textit{Morton v. Mancari}, 417 U.S. 535 (1974), classifications tied to tribal membership are political, not racial. The foster parents reply that a preference for families of any tribe looks less like a political tie to the child's own tribe and more like ancestry. Justice Kavanaugh called the issue ``serious,'' and the Court has not resolved it.

Key Quotations.src: ``To be clear, however, `plenary' does not mean `free-floating.' A power unmoored from the Constitution would lack both justification and limits. So like the rest of its legislative powers, Congress's authority to regulate Indians must derive from the Constitution, not the atmosphere.''

``It could not be otherwise---Article I gives Congress a series of enumerated powers, not a series of blank checks. Thus, we reiterate that Congress's authority to legislate with respect to Indians is not unbounded. It is plenary within its sphere, but even a sizeable sphere has borders. \ldots{} But the Constitution does not erect a firewall around family law.''

``It is a federal court's judgment, not its opinion, that remedies an injury; thus it is the judgment, not the opinion, that demonstrates redressability. The individual petitioners can hope for nothing more than an opinion, so they cannot satisfy Article III.''

``Our Constitution reserves for the Tribes a place---an enduring place---in the structure of American life. It promises them sovereignty for as long as they wish to keep it. And it secures that promise by divesting States of authority over Indian affairs and by giving the federal government certain significant (but limited and enumerated) powers aimed at building a lasting peace.''
